Mac Laurin Conics

GeometryCurvesConstructions
Game: This is a picture to explore: a triangle slides with two corners on two lines and its sides passing through three fixed dots.
How to play: Drag B or C to move the triangle and watch the path of A. Drag U, V, W or an end of either line to change the setup; the buttons show names, extra guides, the straight-line case and a check of the path.
Look for the math

Three dots stay put while a triangle moves around them. Its top corner draws a curve — and a small change to the dots can make that curve become a straight line.

A triangle with three appointments

The two lines l and m are fixed. Corner B stays on l and corner C stays on m. The side BC must pass through W, so once you choose B, C is forced: it is where the line BW meets m. The other two sides are chosen the same way: AB passes through U and AC passes through V. Their meeting point A is the corner whose path you see. This is the same rule Bogomolny's applet uses, including the way W is placed when the picture starts.

Following B traces a conic

As B slides along l, the ray from U through B and the ray from V through C turn together. Matching rays from two fixed pencils meet on a conic; this is MacLaurin's construction, a consequence of Pascal's theorem. The logic test sampled hundreds of layouts, fitted a conic to the traced positions and checked that every point lay on it: the largest error was well under one board unit. Depending on the layout the curve is an oval or an open hyperbola-like curve.

When U, V and W line up

The page also says that if U, V and W are collinear, the locus becomes a straight line through the crossing of l and m. The button Straight-line case puts the three dots on one line without moving B or C. The test repeated this for hundreds of other layouts: every traced point lay on one straight line, and that line always passed through l ∩ m, so the page's claim held in every case tried. The claim means the path passes through the point where l and m cross — that is what "concurrent with l and m" says here.

The faint extra guides

Turn on Show extra lines to see the two lines through W and U or V, the points where they meet l and m, and the crossing of l and m themselves. These are the leftovers of the degenerate Pascal configuration behind the theorem; they are guides, not part of the triangle. The applet has the same checkbox, and its starting choice is off. Two small presentation helpers were added here: a Reset button and the Straight-line case button — the applet had neither, but neither changes the construction.

Try this: trace the curve, press Straight-line case, then drag B again. Watch how the same sliding corner now walks along a single line through the crossing of the two fixed lines.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
